description: Team of 5 innovative high school students at Longfields Davidson Heights
summary:
Martian Pathfinder is an interactive planning tool designed to helps astronauts safely navigate through the Jezero Crater of Mars.
The tool uses layered mapping to show various data from several NASA missions on one site that can be toggled simultaneously. The map also shows the path taken from the Perseverance rover, and which samples it collected at which sites. Our site finds the optimal route for astronauts, accounting for steepness, walk-back time, unstable terrain and suit parameters such as oxygen, water and battery levels. Once a route is generated, users recieve a safety assessment indicating whether their expedition is safe, possible, or dangerous. The pathfinder offers premade missions to gather geologic samples and provides a 3D visualization of the proposed route, helping astronauts better understand the obstacles they may encounter. By combining real NASA mission data, intelligent route optimization as well as an interactive 3D visualization, Martian Pathfinder aims to make future human exploration on Mars more safe and efficient.
details:
Martian Pathfinder is a route planner on Jezero Crater on Mars, where NASA’s Perseverance rover has been exploring. This tool is capable of stacking 15 map layers from NASA mission data; terrain, slope hazards, sand, minerals, dust and more. Martian Pathfinder shows every site where Perseverance collected a sample, including the sample names, rock types, and names. There are certain factors that our tool considers when assessing risk. Factors include daylight, EVA time, terrain hazards, suit consumables and temperature. Based on these factors, our tool determines the risk level of the mission, and assigns it a level: Go, Caution, or No-Go.

Our tool is beneficial because it combines separately recorded NASA data into one accessible menu. Astronauts can simulate potential experiences outside of the habitat in a matter of seconds. Every piece of data states where it is sourced from, and any assumptions are labelled to be assumptions. It also runs in a web browser, free of any installations. 

Our intention is to build a tool that helps future crews plan walks on Mars safely while efficiently completing their objectives. While creating this, we were also able to give students and the public a hands-on, interactive way to explore Mars’s terrain.

To build our project, we’ve used HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the site itself and Powershell for the data. Some libraries we used are Leaflet for the map, three.js for the 3D visualization, geotiff.js for reading the terrain and gdal3.js for converting the USGS geologic map. For our data sources, we’ve used NASA Mars Trek, NASA’s Planetary Data System, USGS Astrogeology, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the NASA Mars Fact Sheet. Some of the mission data we’ve used to help build our project were Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE, CTX, CRISM), Mars Odyssey (THEMIS), Mars Global Surveyor (MOLA, TES), Mars 2020 Perseverance (track, samples, MEDA weather), Curiosity (RAD radiation) and Viking. We used GitHub to host our project’s site, and Anthropic’s Claude to help with coding and site building. 

Our project creatively considers risk factors to determine the safety of a route far before an astronaut ever leaves the habitat or capsule. The stops on the map are also Perseverance’s real sample sites, so astronauts can utilize it to pick up after the rover or collect the tubes it left off. We’ve used NASA’s own data from walking tests for walking times and consumables in our planner. Currently, there’s no way to update Mars’s temperature, wind and dust in real time. For now, we’ve used data from past years to add wind and dust layers on our map. As human expansion on Mars progresses, we plan to incorporate real-time weather data into our Pathfinder tool, as it can provide much more accurate, time relevant risk assessments and efficient route planning. In the 3D model, the sun’s position is simulated as well.

Safety and efficiency are the two main factors we’ve considered during this project. We’ve added a strict steepness limit of 15 degrees, a walk-back limit of 2 hours, reserve levels for consumables, as well as considering the most time efficient routes to complete objectives. All data we use has a traceable source that can be checked at any time by anyone. For data gaps, such as weather, wind, and radiation, the tool states that it’s an assumption. The suit and walking data come from the Moon’s gravity tests, which is also stated in the tool. In addition, we’ve made the site easy to use, with panels, clear buttons and deep explanations.
